content.summary_of_the_paper: In this work, the authors combine several concepts together, including centralized federated learning, decentralized federated learning, and adaptive learning rate. The authors establish the linear speedup property for the proposed method with respect to the number of clients and local iterations. Preliminary experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The authors propose a mixed communication topology by combining decentralized and centralized federated learning. Before this work is accepted, several issues should be resolved:
(i)	The motivation is not clear. Does the “dilemma of local steps” mainly come from the adaptive learning rate? In each cluster, the authors apply decentralized SGD to accelerate local training. To my knowledge, the convergence rate of decentralized SGD is the same as centralized SGD. Thus, in each cluster, the decentralized training maybe not be necessary and centralized SGD could also resolve the ‘dilemma of local steps’. Hence, the motivation for introducing the hybrid structure is not clear. We may recommend the authors conduct more experiments to verify their motivations. 
(ii)	The comparison is unfair. We agree with the comment “without extra client-to-server communication”. In federated learning, the clients could be IoT devices, which have low bandwidth. The main burden may exist in the local devices. Thus, due to the intra-cluster decentralized training, each client needs to communicate with its neighborhoods, which also requires communication costs. For a fair comparison, we recommend the authors compare the preference with respect to the number of communication rounds of each client, rather than the server. 
(iii)	The “dilemma of local steps” needs further verifications. The largest local steps are set as 96 and the local minibatch size is 50. Thus, the local training is less than 3 epochs, which is still a small length of the local interval. We recommend the authors increase \tau to 1, 2,5,10 epochs of local training to check the dilemma of local steps. 
(iv)	More baselines are required. Recently, several new optimizers have been proposed for federated learning. We recommend the authors compare their proposed optimizers with new SOTA baselines, including FedSAM, FedCM, SCAFFOLD, and FedDyn. 
(v)	In Figure 1(a), the convergence curve of FedAMSGrad does not converge. We recommend the authors increase the communication rounds to 1000 to check the final acc of HA-Fed and FedAMSGrad.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes HA-FED, a federated learning algorithm that tries to accelerate the adaptive algorithms like Adam and RMSprop using the local gossip steps. Theoretically, this paper shows that the local gossip steps help the convergence and alleviate the data heterogeneity issue. Numerical experiments are presented to show the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. This paper tries to use the local gossip steps as a substitution for the pure local steps, which tries to alleviate the problem brought by the data heterogeneity issue and pure local steps.
2. The experiment results show that the proposed algorithm indeed works better than the previous adaptive optimization algorithms for federated learning.

Weakness:

1. For the theoretical analysis, this paper uses the very strong bounded gradient assumption, which is understandable for analyzing adaptive optimization algorithms. However, this bounded gradient assumption directly conflicts with the data heterogeneity, since bounded gradient leads to bounded dissimilarity and thus it should not be a big issue in theory. Thus, I am not convinced by the story of this paper.
2. Although the authors claim that they also have the partial participation version of the algorithm, the algorithm (in the appendix) actually needs to communicate with every cluster at the same time: it is more like the full participation case, since in the extreme case if the cluster is fully connected, then communicating with every cluster is very similar to communicating with all the clients. This assumption may not be practical in real use cases like the IoT settings which have data heterogeneity.
3. The experiment does not try the extreme case in the heterogeneous data setting. In the Appendix, the data partition for the non-iid setting is to partition each label into bins and the clients/agents/devices randomly select the bins. I am not fully convinced that this setting can simulate the heterogeneous data: to me, it is just a little bit more heterogeneous than purely random shuffle, but it does not make a huge difference. To simulate the full heterogeneous data setting, one should try to fully sort the dataset and assign them to clients, or at least make a portion of them fully sorted.
4. There is a paper "Accelerating gossip SGD with periodic global averaging" by Chen et al. 2021 that basically has the same idea: using global fed-avg to accelerate local gossip communication. It can also be understood as accelerating fed-avg using local gossip communication. It appears in the citation of the paper but the author seems to forget to mention the idea or compare the results with this paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The paper is clearly written, except the authors forgot to have more discussion with the paper "Accelerating gossip SGD with periodic global averaging" by Chen et al. 2021, which has a very similar idea.

Quality:
The empirical part shows some interesting results. The proof of the theoretical part should be correct (it at least makes sense to me). From my perspective, this paper is a solid paper.

Novelty:
Given the paper "Accelerating gossip SGD with periodic global averaging" by Chen et al. 2021, I don't think this paper has much novelty.

Reproducibility:
Can be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Please see the strength and weaknesses part for more details. 

Based on the weaknesses I found, I feel like this paper does not reach the acceptance standard. I hope that the authors can alleviate my concerns in the weaknesses part.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This submission considers the federated optimization problem with local gossip communication applied for updating client models and adaptive gradient method applied for updating server model. The authors provide theoretical proof for convergence guarantee in terms of first-order condition, and benchmark the proposed algorithm with FedAMSGrad.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

-> The paper is clearly structured, and the study is comprehensive.

-> Tacking the dilemma of local steps is a very important target for the general community, which I very much appreciate.

Weaknesses:

-> The theoretical proof does not seem to directly support the proposed algorithm.

-> Some numerical experiment setup should be further explained.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Regarding algorithm/proof:

-> Throughout the entire section C in appendix, proof for theorem 5.6, it is unexpected that the local communication matrices $W_k$ does not appear at all. Now that the local gossip is an important ingredient in the proposed main algorithm 1, and the theorem 5.6 is claimed to support algorithm 1, it is not evident to me how the general setup of the proof supports algorithm 1.

-> About partial participation, in algorithm 2, if each local cluster is connected, lines 5-7 are not different than full participation case, right?

-> About partial participation, in algorithm 2, should line 9 be "for each client $i \in \mathcal{V}_k \cap \mathcal{S}^k_t$? If the authors mean exactly as what was written in the submitted manuscript, then the sense of 'partial participation' is only limited to data transmission rather than model update and evaluation. This can be seen by line 15, where all clients still upload their local information $\Delta_t^i$ to the server. This is unconventional for the sense of 'partial participation'.

Regarding numerical experiments:

-> I would like to understand better regarding the setup of local clients, and how each local clients are connected to each other. 

-> How about data homogeneity when authors are plotting figure 3? Are data distributions across all clients the same or different? If the data is i.i.d. across all clients, then the performance demonstrated in figure 3 is not that surprising.
content.summary_of_the_review: Some important aspects in the theoretical proof and numerical experiments should be better clarified to justify the claimed result. The current status of the manuscript does incur reasonable doubts about the claimed result.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes changing the architecture of adaptive federated optimization methods to a hybrid model between federated learning and decentralized optimization. Agents are divided into individual clusters in which communication is governed by some network topology. These clusters communicate by having representative agents from each cluster send their model difference to a central server for aggregation. At the aggregation step, the server uses these model differences to perform one step of AMSGrad. Convergence analysis and experimental results are provided.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The analysis of the algorithm requires very strong assumptions. Assumption 5.2 requires that the norm of the stochastic gradient of each agent's objective function is bounded. However, this assumption is false when the function is strongly convex and in other cases such as when $f(x) = \frac{1}{2}(x)^2 + x$, $\mathbb{E} [\lVert f(x, \eta) \rVert^2]$ can be arbitrarily large \cite{nguyen2018hogwild}. In addition, Assumption 5.4, which bounds the variance between the local client's objective function and the objective function of the cluster and bounds the variance between the objective function of the cluster and the global objective function, indicates that the algorithm is not bias-correcting. Hence, as seen in the analysis, there is a bias term ($\phi_1$) proportional to these variances. The analysis of the algorithm also provides no bound on the global step size $\eta$ or the adapative parameter $\epsilon$. $C$ and $C_0$ are also both not defined with a statement that they are irrelevant to the parameters. $d$ is also not defined. These considerations play an important role when we consider that the step size is inversely proportional to the heterogeneity through $\alpha$ or the $G$-bounded stochastic gradient. To get the desired rate $O (1/\sqrt{T\tau N})$ the analysis suggests choosing $\eta = \Theta(\sqrt{\tau N})$ and $\eta_l = \Theta(1/\sqrt{T\tau^2})$ when $T$ is sufficiently large, i.e., $T > \tau N$. However, it is unclear to the reviewer how the requirement $T > \tau N$ is independent of the data heterogeneity terms $\alpha$, $ \sigma^2_k$, and $\sigma^2_g$ as well as the bounded gradient term $G$, all substantial quantities. 

The experiments through the design are insufficient. There is no indication of how the datasets are distributed among the agents. If there datasets are distributed in an i.i.d fashion increasing the number of local steps as in Figure 3 would immediately lead to a faster result. In addition, no hyperparameters whatsoever are provided making it impossible to replicate the experiments. Figure 2 does not support the author's claims. A larger participation ratio should improve the training loss. A smaller $\rho_{\max}$ should improve the training loss. The results in Figure 2 are marginal at best if not entirely insignificant. Having such a wide discrepancy despite vastly changing the participation ratio $p$ and the maximum spectral gap of a cluster indicates that there is a critical issue with the experiment design leading back to the reviewers thoughts that agents each have data from the same distribution. In addition, providing the step-size used to compare the number of local steps is crucial as the best possible local step-size should be chosen. This is important because the local step-size is inversely proportional to the number of local steps and, hence, should be scaled accordingly. If one chose a constant step-size across all choices of local steps such that convergence is achieved, that step-size maybe be too conservative for smaller number of local steps.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity and quality of the paper is extremely poor. Constants such as $C$ and $d$ are not defined. Bounds on terms such as $\epsilon$ and $\eta$ are also not defined. The work is not very novel. The hybrid model proposed by this work is the same exact model used in (Guo,2022). The only difference is the addition of an adaptive step when performing global aggregation. The reproducibility of the experiments is extremely low as none of the hyperparameters such as the local step-sizes are provided and the process of distributing data is not well defined.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper modifies the hybrid federated learning model detailed in (Guo,2022) by adding an adaptive step when performing global aggregation. Convergence analysis and experiments are performed.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
